subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: An infant presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. An upper GI series shows the small bowel clumped on the right side of the abdomen and the colon located on the left. At surgery, fibrous bands are found crossing from the right colon to the duodenum, and the midgut has twisted around its mesenteric pedicle.
question: Which of the following best explains this infant's presentation?

options.text: A persistent vitelline duct with ectopic gastric mucosa in the ileum
Aganglionosis of the distal colon with a transition zone
Telescoping of the ileum into the cecum with a Peyer patch lead point
Abnormal midgut rotation with Ladd bands causing duodenal obstruction and volvulus
A colonic false diverticulum with pericolic inflammation

explanation_correct: Malrotation is an anomaly of midgut rotation during fetal development, producing improper bowel positioning (small bowel on the right, colon on the left) and formation of fibrous Ladd bands. These bands can cause duodenal obstruction, and the abnormally based mesentery predisposes to midgut volvulus with bilious vomiting—a surgical emergency in infants.

explanation_incorrect.A: A persistent vitelline duct is Meckel diverticulum, which can cause painless bleeding or act as an intussusception lead point but does not produce the abnormal bowel position and Ladd bands seen here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Aganglionosis of the distal colon is Hirschsprung disease, which causes delayed meconium and a transition zone, not right-sided small bowel with a twisted mesentery.
explanation_incorrect.C: Telescoping of ileum into cecum with a Peyer patch lead point describes intussusception, which causes currant jelly stools and a target sign, not the fixed malposition of malrotation.
explanation_incorrect.E: A colonic false diverticulum with pericolic inflammation is diverticulitis of older adults, not a congenital midgut rotational abnormality in an infant.

educationalObjective: Malrotation causes abnormal midgut position and Ladd bands that can lead to duodenal obstruction and midgut volvulus with bilious vomiting.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: An 8-month-old infant has episodes of severe, intermittent abdominal pain during which the child screams and draws the legs up to the chest. Between episodes the infant is lethargic. Physical examination reveals a sausage-shaped mass in the right abdomen, and the stool is described as currant jelly. An ultrasound shows a target sign.
question: Which of the following best explains this infant's findings?

options.text: Telescoping of a proximal bowel segment into a distal segment at the ileocecal junction
Twisting of the sigmoid colon around its mesentery with a coffee bean sign
Necrosis of the terminal ileum with portal venous gas in a premature infant
A colovesical fistula complicating sigmoid diverticulitis
Ischemic injury at the splenic flexure watershed area

explanation_correct: Intussusception is the telescoping of a proximal bowel segment into a distal segment, most commonly at the ileocecal junction, and is typically seen in infants. It causes intermittent abdominal pain with the child drawing the legs to the chest, a sausage-shaped mass, vomiting, and currant jelly stools from vascular compromise; ultrasound or CT shows a target sign. The idiopathic form is associated with recent viral infection and Peyer patch hypertrophy.

explanation_incorrect.B: Sigmoid volvulus with a coffee bean sign occurs in older adults, not infants, and produces distention rather than a sausage mass and currant jelly stools.
explanation_incorrect.C: Necrotizing enterocolitis affects premature, formula-fed infants with pneumatosis and portal venous gas, not a target sign or a palpable sausage mass.
explanation_incorrect.D: A colovesical fistula complicates diverticulitis in older adults and causes pneumaturia, not intermittent pain and currant jelly stools in an infant.
explanation_incorrect.E: Colonic ischemia at the splenic flexure occurs in older adults with crampy pain and hematochezia, not in an infant with a target sign on ultrasound.

educationalObjective: Intussusception in infants is ileocecal telescoping causing colicky pain, a sausage mass, currant jelly stools, and a target sign.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: Three patients present with intussusception: a 9-month-old infant recovering from adenovirus gastroenteritis, an 8-year-old child with IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), and a 67-year-old man with weight loss and a palpable abdominal mass. The clinician considers what serves as the lead point in each age group.
question: Which of the following correctly matches the likely lead point to each patient?

options.text: Infant—colonic tumor; child—Meckel diverticulum; adult—Peyer patch hypertrophy
Infant—small bowel hematoma; child—intraluminal tumor; adult—Meckel diverticulum
Infant—hypertrophied Peyer patch after viral infection; child—Meckel diverticulum or bowel wall hematoma; adult—intraluminal tumor
Infant—Meckel diverticulum; child—rotavirus vaccine; adult—IgA vasculitis
Infant—intraluminal tumor; child—adenovirus; adult—bowel wall hematoma

explanation_correct: The idiopathic infantile form is associated with recent viral infections (eg, adenovirus) and rotavirus vaccine, with Peyer patch hypertrophy acting as a lead point. In children, identifiable lead points include Meckel diverticulum and small bowel wall hematoma from IgA vasculitis; in adults, an intraluminal mass or tumor is the classic lead point. Option C matches all three age groups correctly.

explanation_incorrect.A: Colonic tumors are adult lead points, not infant ones, and Peyer patch hypertrophy is associated with infantile idiopathic disease after viral infection, not adults.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bowel wall hematoma is a childhood lead point (IgA vasculitis), and intraluminal tumor is an adult lead point; the infant's lead point is a hypertrophied Peyer patch.
explanation_incorrect.D: Meckel diverticulum is a childhood lead point rather than the typical infantile one, rotavirus vaccine is associated with idiopathic infantile disease rather than being a lead point itself, and IgA vasculitis causes hematomas in children.
explanation_incorrect.E: Intraluminal tumors are adult, not infant, lead points; adenovirus is associated with idiopathic infantile disease via Peyer patch hypertrophy, and bowel wall hematoma is a childhood rather than adult lead point.

educationalObjective: Intussusception lead points: Peyer patch hypertrophy in infants after viral illness, Meckel diverticulum or hematoma in children, and intraluminal tumor in adults.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A clinician reviews three cases of volvulus, defined as twisting of a portion of bowel around its mesentery with risk of obstruction and infarction. One is an adult with a paraesophageal hernia, severe abdominal pain, dry heaving, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube. Another is a toddler with midgut twisting. The third is an 82-year-old with constipation and a coffee bean sign on abdominal x-ray.
question: Which of the following correctly assigns the type of volvulus to each patient?

options.text: Adult—sigmoid volvulus; toddler—gastric volvulus; elderly—midgut volvulus
Adult—midgut volvulus; toddler—sigmoid volvulus; elderly—gastric volvulus
Adult—gastric volvulus; toddler—sigmoid volvulus; elderly—midgut volvulus
Adult—midgut volvulus; toddler—gastric volvulus; elderly—sigmoid volvulus
Adult—gastric volvulus; toddler—midgut volvulus; elderly—sigmoid volvulus

explanation_correct: Gastric volvulus is more common in adults with abnormalities such as a paraesophageal hernia and presents with severe pain, dry heaving, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube. Midgut volvulus is more common in infants and children (minors). Sigmoid volvulus is more common in older adults (seniors) and shows a coffee bean sign on x-ray. Option E assigns all three correctly.

explanation_incorrect.A: The adult with a paraesophageal hernia has gastric, not sigmoid, volvulus; the toddler has midgut, not gastric, volvulus; and the elderly patient with a coffee bean sign has sigmoid, not midgut, volvulus.
explanation_incorrect.B: Midgut volvulus is a disease of infants/children rather than adults, sigmoid volvulus affects seniors rather than toddlers, and gastric volvulus is associated with adult paraesophageal hernia rather than the elderly patient described.
explanation_incorrect.C: The adult is correctly assigned gastric volvulus, but the toddler has midgut volvulus, not sigmoid, and the elderly patient has sigmoid volvulus (coffee bean sign), not midgut.
explanation_incorrect.D: The adult's paraesophageal hernia and dry heaving indicate gastric volvulus, not midgut; the toddler's midgut volvulus is incorrectly labeled gastric.

educationalObjective: Volvulus types by age: gastric with paraesophageal hernia in adults, midgut in infants/children, and sigmoid with coffee bean sign in seniors.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has had a large portion of her distal ileum resected during surgery for Crohn disease. She now develops voluminous postprandial diarrhea, dehydration, and weight loss. Laboratory evaluation shows anemia, and imaging reveals calcium oxalate kidney stones.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's diarrhea and kidney stones?

options.text: Loss of gastric parietal cells causing pernicious anemia and achlorhydria
Malabsorption of bile salts and fat at the distal ileum after resection
Excess gastric acid secretion from a gastrinoma
Small bacterial overgrowth from a blind loop without any resection
Colonic false diverticula with recurrent painless hematochezia

explanation_correct: Short bowel syndrome follows significant surgical resection (eg, for Crohn disease, malignancy, or trauma) and causes inability to absorb nutrients. Loss of the distal ileum produces malabsorption of bile salts and fat, leading to voluminous postprandial diarrhea, dehydration, weight loss, anemia, and calcium oxalate kidney stones—the latter because unabsorbed fat binds calcium, leaving oxalate to be absorbed.

explanation_incorrect.A: Loss of gastric parietal cells causes pernicious anemia with achlorhydria, but it does not produce the postprandial fat and bile salt diarrhea or calcium oxalate stones of distal ileal resection.
explanation_incorrect.C: A gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) causes excess gastric acid with refractory ulcers and diarrhea, not the malabsorption that follows surgical loss of ileal absorptive surface.
explanation_incorrect.D: Small bowel bacterial overgrowth can occur with a blind loop and cause B12 malabsorption, but the key mechanism here is the resection-related loss of ileal bile salt and fat absorption.
explanation_incorrect.E: Colonic false diverticula (diverticulosis) cause painless hematochezia in older adults, not the diarrhea, dehydration, and oxalate stones of short bowel syndrome.

educationalObjective: Distal ileal resection causes short bowel syndrome with bile salt and fat malabsorption, voluminous diarrhea, and calcium oxalate stones.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: An 81-year-old man with chronic constipation presents with abdominal distention and vomiting. An abdominal x-ray shows a dilated loop of colon in the shape of a coffee bean, with the apex pointing toward the left upper quadrant. There is no air in the rectum, and he has no prior abdominal surgery.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acute mesenteric ischemia from embolic SMA occlusion
Sigmoid volvulus
Adhesive small bowel obstruction
Adynamic ileus from opiate use
Colonic ischemia at the rectosigmoid watershed

explanation_correct: Sigmoid volvulus is twisting of the sigmoid colon around its mesentery, more common in older adults (seniors), and classically produces a dilated coffee bean-shaped loop on abdominal x-ray with obstruction. This patient's age, constipation, distention, and characteristic imaging are classic for sigmoid volvulus, a form of volvulus that can lead to obstruction and infarction.

explanation_incorrect.A: Acute mesenteric ischemia from SMA embolism causes pain out of proportion to findings and currant jelly stools in patients with atrial fibrillation or vascular disease, not a coffee bean loop.
explanation_incorrect.C: Adhesive small bowel obstruction causes air-fluid levels and proximal dilation with distal decompression, usually after prior surgery, which this patient lacks.
explanation_incorrect.D: Adynamic ileus from opiates causes diffuse hypomotility, reduced flatus, and decreased bowel sounds without a transition zone or a coffee bean-shaped loop.
explanation_incorrect.E: Colonic ischemia at the rectosigmoid watershed causes crampy pain followed by hematochezia with a thumbprint sign on imaging, not a twisted coffee bean loop.

educationalObjective: Sigmoid volvulus occurs in older adults and is identified by a coffee bean-shaped dilated colon on abdominal x-ray.
